prompt: In `app.py`, the line `LOADED = time.time()` sits outside the handler. When does it run?

choices.text: Once per execution environment, at import
choices.why: The runtime imports the file once, in the INIT phase, and every later event in that environment reuses what it set.

choices.text: Before every event, just ahead of the handler
choices.why: Then `warm_for_s` would be near zero on every call; in the capture it grew between the first two.

choices.text: Once when the function is created with `create-function`
choices.why: Creating a function stores a package; no code runs until an environment imports it.

choices.text: After the handler returns, while the environment is frozen
choices.why: A frozen environment runs nothing at all; the line ran before the first event.

prompt: A function's configuration says `--handler greet.handler`, and its zip holds only `app.py` with `def handler`. What happens at the first invocation?

choices.text: Lambda finds the only function called `handler` and runs it
choices.why: The handler name is a path, file then function. Nothing searches the package for a function by name.

choices.text: `create-function` should already have refused it
choices.why: Neither moto nor AWS imports the code at creation; the mismatch only shows when an environment starts.

choices.text: A `Runtime.ImportModuleError`: there is no `greet` module
choices.why: The runtime tries to import `greet` from `/var/task` and fails before any event is handled, as `shop` did without its layer.

choices.text: The event is passed to `app.py` as a script
choices.why: Lambda never runs a file as a script; it imports a module and calls a function in it.

prompt: A `REPORT` line says `Duration: 37.20 ms`. Going by the rule the emulator's log showed, what `Billed Duration` does Lambda charge, in milliseconds?
hint: In the capture, 1.05 ms was billed as 2 ms.

prompt: Every `REPORT` from the emulator ended in `Memory Size: 3008 MB Max Memory Used: 3008 MB`. What should you conclude about your function's memory on AWS?

choices.text: It needs 3008 MB, so configure that much
choices.why: It used nothing like that: the emulator repeats the size it was given instead of measuring.

choices.text: Nothing; both figures are the emulator's defaults
choices.why: The emulator gives every function 3008 MB and reports the same number as used. Lambda measures `Max Memory Used`, and on AWS that line means something.

choices.text: It leaks memory, since it used all of it
choices.why: A function that used all its memory on Lambda would be stopped with an out-of-memory error; this one returned normally.

choices.text: Lambda will give it 3008 MB, its default
choices.why: Lambda's default is 128 MB, as `create-function` showed in moto; 3008 MB is the emulator's.

prompt: Lambda unpacks a function's own package into the directory `/var/___`, which is where the emulator had the code mounted.
The first `create-function` failed with `The role defined for the function cannot be assumed by Lambda.` What was missing?

choices.text: A permission policy allowing `lambda:CreateFunction`
choices.why: moto evaluates no IAM policies by default, so the caller's permissions were not what failed.

choices.text: A runtime that supports roles
choices.why: Every runtime runs with an execution role; it is not a feature of some of them.

choices.text: A zip whose `app.py` is inside a folder named after the role
choices.why: The role has nothing to do with the zip's layout, and `app.py` belongs at the root.

choices.text: The role itself, trusting `lambda.amazonaws.com`
choices.why: `greet-role` did not exist yet. Once created with a trust policy naming the Lambda service, the same call worked.

prompt: A function created with Lambda's defaults has a timeout of 3 seconds; the emulator's `remaining_ms` started near 300,000. How many times longer is the emulator's timeout?
`aws lambda invoke` against moto answered `"StatusCode": 200` and `"FunctionError": "Handled"`, and `out.json` began `error running docker`. What failed?

choices.text: The handler raised `ValueError`
choices.why: That would need the handler to run. Here no runtime started, because moto could not fetch an image to start one in.

choices.text: Nothing: a status of 200 means the call succeeded
choices.why: Lambda answers 200 for a function that failed and says so in `FunctionError`; reading only the status hides every error.

choices.text: The role lacked permission to write logs
choices.why: A missing log permission does not stop a handler from running or returning; the error text names Docker.

choices.text: moto's attempt to pull a runtime image from Docker Hub
choices.why: moto runs a handler in a community image it pulls, and this machine could not pull it. AWS's own image, in the emulator, is how the course runs code.

prompt: On AWS, `create-function --zip-file fileb://big.zip` with a 60 MB zip is refused. The code unzips to 140 MB. What is the way to deploy it as a zip?

choices.text: Upload it to S3 and pass `--code S3Bucket=…,S3Key=…`
choices.why: The 50 MB limit is on a zip sent in the request. From S3 the zip may be larger, and 140 MB unzipped is under the 250 MB limit.

choices.text: Split it into two functions of 30 MB each
choices.why: That changes the application to fit a transport limit that has a simpler way round it.

choices.text: Compress it harder, since only the unzipped size counts
choices.why: The direct upload is limited by the zip's own size, and random-looking content does not compress.

choices.text: Nothing works below 250 MB zipped; use an image
choices.why: An image is an option, but not the only one: below 250 MB unzipped, a zip from S3 is accepted.

prompt: Put in order the steps that take an edit of `app.py` to a version of the function that will never change again.
items: Zip it again, with app.py at the root
trap: Publishing a version before updating the code freezes the old package: a version copies whatever $LATEST holds at that moment.

prompt: A colleague builds the layer with `zip ../shopfmt.zip shopfmt.py`, the module at the root of the zip. The function then fails with `No module named 'shopfmt'`. Why?

choices.text: Layers have to be published for arm64
choices.why: The architecture of a pure Python module makes no difference; it is where the file landed.

choices.text: The function names `shopfmt:1` instead of `shopfmt:$LATEST`
choices.why: Layers have no `$LATEST`; a function always names a numbered version.

choices.text: A layer's modules are imported only after the handler starts
choices.why: Imports happen at INIT, from `/var/task` and then the layer's directories; there is no later pass.

choices.text: It lands in `/opt/shopfmt.py`, and the runtime imports from `/opt/python`
choices.why: Lambda unpacks the zip into `/opt` as it is, and the Python runtime only adds `/opt/python` to its path.

prompt: Which of these belong in a layer rather than in the function's own package? Choose every one the section argues for.

choices.text: `shopfmt`, used by several functions
choices.why: A shared library is what a layer is for: one copy to publish and update.

choices.text: A large dependency that rarely changes
choices.why: It keeps the function's own zip small, so every upload of the code is quick.

choices.text: A monitoring extension for `/opt/extensions`
choices.why: Extensions are delivered as layers, into the directory the runtime looks in.

choices.text: The handler file itself
choices.why: The handler changes with every commit and belongs to one function; it goes in that function's package.

choices.text: A dependency that only one function uses
choices.why: Sharing it with nobody gains nothing, and costs a second thing to version.

prompt: `shopfmt:2` is published with a bug. Twelve functions use `shopfmt`, and two of them were moved to version 2 this morning. Which functions break?

choices.text: The two that name version 2
choices.why: Layer versions are immutable and each function keeps the one it names, so the other ten still run `shopfmt:1`.

choices.text: All twelve, as soon as version 2 exists
choices.why: A function names a layer version; publishing a new one changes no function's configuration.

choices.text: The ten still on version 1, which AWS retires
choices.why: Publishing a version retires nothing; version 1 stays until somebody deletes it.

choices.text: None until each function's `$LATEST` is published again
choices.why: The two moved functions run the new layer at once; their configuration changed when they were moved.

prompt: A function's own package unzips to 180 MB. To get under the limit, a colleague moves 90 MB of it into a layer. What does AWS do?

choices.text: It accepts it: 90 MB of package and 90 MB of layer
choices.why: The limit is not per piece. The function and its layers are counted together.

choices.text: It accepts it, since layers live in `/opt`
choices.why: Where the files land does not matter to the quota; `/var/task` and `/opt` share the 250 MB.

choices.text: Nothing changes: still 180 MB, still allowed
choices.why: Moving bytes into a layer neither adds nor removes them, and 180 MB is under 250 MB, so the move was never needed.

choices.text: It refuses, because a layer may hold at most 50 MB
choices.why: 50 MB is the limit on a zip uploaded directly, for a function or a layer, not on what a layer may hold unzipped.

prompt: A function's package unzips to 140 MB and it names two layers of 60 MB and 35 MB, unzipped. How many MB are left under Lambda's limit for one more layer?
hint: The function and every layer are counted together.

prompt: With the sheet's prices of 16 October 2026, what does a month cost on Arm for six million invocations of a 512 MB function running 200 ms each, requests included and the free allowance left out? Answer in USD.
hint: GB-seconds are invocations × seconds × GB; requests are 0.2 USD per million.

prompt: moto created a function with `--runtime python3.99`. What would AWS have done with the same call?

choices.text: Created it on the newest Python available
choices.why: AWS does not round a runtime name to the nearest one; a name that is not on its list is an error.

choices.text: Created it, then failed at the first invocation
choices.why: The name is checked when the function is created, not when it first runs.

choices.text: Refused it with `InvalidParameterValueException`
choices.why: `python3.99` has never existed, and AWS answers with the error and the names it accepts.

choices.text: Created it as a deprecated runtime with no patches
choices.why: Deprecation applies to runtimes that existed; a name that never existed cannot be deprecated.

prompt: A function has been on a runtime since before its deprecation date, and nobody has touched it. What is its state after that date?

choices.text: It keeps running, without security patches
choices.why: Deprecation stops the patches and, later, creation and updates; invocations go on.

choices.text: AWS moves it to the next runtime version automatically
choices.why: Automatic updates stay within the same runtime; moving to a new language version is a change the owner makes.

choices.text: It stops answering on the deprecation date
choices.why: Nothing in AWS's three steps stops a running function; that is why an unowned function on an old runtime is a risk rather than an outage.

choices.text: It is converted to a container image of the same runtime
choices.why: No such conversion exists; an image is something the owner builds and deploys.

prompt: The resizer works on x86. After `--architectures arm64` and the same zip, every invocation fails importing a compiled image library. What is the fix?

choices.text: Raise the memory, since Arm needs more of it
choices.why: Memory does not change which processor a compiled file was built for.

choices.text: Build the package again with the library's arm64 wheel
choices.why: A compiled dependency is built for one architecture, so the package has to be made for the one it runs on.

choices.text: Move the library into a layer, which Lambda translates for Arm
choices.why: Lambda unpacks a layer as it is; it translates nothing, so an x86 file fails from `/opt` exactly as from `/var/task`.

choices.text: Switch the runtime to `provided.al2023`
choices.why: That runtime is for a function that brings its own runtime; it does not change the architecture of a library.

prompt: Match each runtime name with what it gives a function.

pairs.right: Python 3.12 on Amazon Linux 2023, patched by AWS
Amazon Linux 2023 and a runtime the function brings, as Go does

right_distractors: A container image of up to 10 GB
Python 3.12 that AWS no longer patches

prompt: A team deploys the same handler as a container image built `FROM public.ecr.aws/lambda/python:3.12`, instead of a zip on `python3.12`. Who patches the runtime now?

choices.text: AWS, underneath the running function, as with a zip
choices.why: That is a managed runtime's arrangement. In an image the runtime is part of what you built.

choices.text: ECR, which rescans and patches stored images
choices.why: ECR stores and scans images; it does not rewrite them.

choices.text: Nobody: an image's runtime never needs patches
choices.why: An image carries the same operating system and Python as the zip's runtime, with the same need for fixes.

choices.text: The team, by rebuilding from a newer base image and deploying it
choices.why: The image holds the runtime, so patches arrive only when the image is rebuilt and the function updated.

prompt: A handler opens a database connection at module level, next to `LOADED`. A hundred events arrive one after another and one environment handles them all. How many connections were opened?

choices.text: A hundred, one per event
choices.why: That is what opening it inside the handler would do. At module level it runs at INIT only.

choices.text: One, made at INIT and reused by every event
choices.why: Module-level code runs once per environment, which is why it is the place for a connection or a client worth reusing.

choices.text: None until the first event asks for one
choices.why: Module-level code does not wait for an event; it runs when the file is imported.

choices.text: Two, one at INIT and one for the first event
choices.why: Nothing runs the module twice in the same environment.

prompt: A handler caches a downloaded file in `/var/task/cache.json`, and every invocation on AWS fails writing it. Where should the cache go?

choices.text: `/opt`, where the layers are
choices.why: `/opt` is read-only like `/var/task`; both hold what was unpacked from your zips.

choices.text: Into the zip, so it arrives already written
choices.why: That works only for a file that never changes; a cache of downloads is written at run time.

choices.text: `/var/runtime`, beside the runtime
choices.why: That directory is AWS's runtime, and a function does not write there.

choices.text: `/tmp`
choices.why: It is the one writable directory, 512 MB by default, and it lasts as long as the environment does.

prompt: A handler returns `{'tags': {'a', 'b'}}`, a dictionary holding a Python set. What does the caller receive?

choices.text: The tags as a JSON list
choices.why: The runtime does not convert a set; it uses the standard JSON encoder, which has no rule for one.

choices.text: An empty answer with status 200
choices.why: The failure is reported, like the `ValueError` was, as an error object.

choices.text: A `Runtime.MarshalError`, since a set is not JSON
choices.why: What the handler returns must be serialisable to JSON; the runtime reports `Unable to marshal response` when it is not.

choices.text: A Python `repr` string of the dictionary
choices.why: The runtime never falls back to `repr`; the answer is JSON or an error.
